But there are also upside risks to core inflation in March and April, and the degree of pass through from higher energy costs to core inflation will likely not be more apparent until mid-year. Factors influencing our inflation assessment last week: (↑) Import prices excluding petroleum rose a substantial 1.3%MoM in February following a strong 0.8% increase in January. February was the largest one-month increase in import prices since January 2022. Stronger import prices even ahead of higher transportation and input costs reinforce the growing upside risks to goods prices this year from factors other than tariffs. We will continue to watch data like import prices and PPI goods prices for risks of continue strength in consumer goods. But we would note a few caveats that keep us cautious for now to not read too much of a new signal from higher import prices – stronger January/February import prices have not impacted our latest CPI or PCE forecasts. Import prices are reported in non-seasonally adjusted terms and generally also experience the same seasonal patterns as other prices, rising more at the start of the year. Many import prices were also not collected during the government shutdown in October/November. Intuitively, this should naturally lead to a divergence in inflation risk premium with incrementally more downward pressure on EUR HICPx relative to USCPI. records.text: READ OUR PUBLICATIONS ON OUR MOBILE APP What’s changed? The US 2s30s yield curve has been flattening in the past six weeks. The yield curve bull flattened going into the Middle East conflict as popular curve steepeners were taken off, and bear flattened after the conflict started as the focus shifted to the “inflation shock” and the possibility of a more symmetric reaction function at the Fed. In the current set-up, we think the yield curve could steepen in both an escalation scenario and a de- escalation scenario. In an escalation scenario, markets are likely to turn their attention to already high but less-focused-on fiscal risks (and there are many), which should build term premium. In addition, growth risks might get more limelight alongside inflation and, given a high bar for a rate hike, might limit a rise in front-end yields, which have moved a lot already. This will likely steepen or at least limit a flattening of the curve. In a de-escalation, markets are likely to un-price the recent inflation-risk-driven flattening and could go back to pricing an asymmetrically dovish Fed reaction function. See page three for our 2s30s UST steepeners idea. Central clearing promises to reduce systemic risks and enhance dealer balance sheet efficiency, though not without raising specific industry concerns, including higher costs associated with clearing trades to a central counterparty (CCP) , imposed on both the margin and capital fronts. The details around how these issues are addressed will determine the full impact on funding markets. In this note, we focus specifically on how the transition might impact SOFR fixings within the Fed’s target range. Claude’s Reasoning: 1-Year Horizon (2025–2026) At the 1-year horizon, the dominant expectation is that AI will have minimal direct impact on aggregate US inflation (Scenario B, 50%). The reasoning is as follows: • Adoption lags: While ChatGPT and similar tools have achieved rapid user adoption, enterprise-level integration into production processes — the kind that affects unit costs and prices — takes considerably longer. Brynjolfsson, Rock, & Syverson (2021) document a "productivity J-curve" where new general-purpose technologies initially reduce measured productivity as firms invest in complementary intangible capital (reorganization, training, workflow redesign) before benefits emerge. • Small macro footprint: AI-related spending, while growing rapidly, remains a small share of GDP. Total US AI investment (hardware, software, services) is estimated at roughly $150–200 billion annually — significant but under 1% of GDP. Its price-level effects are correspondingly small relative to forces like monetary policy, fiscal policy, and global commodity markets. records.text: of the Japanese economy discussed so far is based primarily on its ability to absorb short-term shocks. If disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz were to extend into the medium term and elevated energy prices were to persist, adverse effects on the economy would be unavoidable. Downside pressures on growth would gradually accumulate through slower exports—particularly to Asia and the Middle East—compressed corporate profits, a decline in households’ real purchasing power, and restraint in investment and consumption. Moreover, in a scenario where Middle East disruptions are prolonged, it is important to be mindful not only of the conventional downside risks to growth, but also of the risk of nonlinear economic deterioration should certain conditions coincide. In particular, close attention should be paid to three factors: (1) supply-chain disruptions originating from tightness in basic chemical products; (2) government-led demand- restraint measures, including a reassessment of gasoline subsidies; and (3) the risk that deteriorating financing conditions for small and medium-sized enterprises spill over into wage growth and employment.

Since the start of the Iran conflict we have cut our year-ahead global growth and inflation forecasts by a more limited amount than these model estimates suggest. GDP growth has been lowered by just 0.2%-pts and CPI inflation forecasts have been raised by 0.7%-pts. Fiscal measures to limit energy pass-through to consumer prices explain a small portion of this gap. The downside risks to this limited adjustment go beyond the model estimates alone. Is the money spent as quickly and efficiently as planned? A recent study by the ifo institute argued that in 2025, (1) German public investment was significantly below plan and (2) that most of the increased borrowing did not end up in infrastructure. What to make of these findings? First, we are not surprised that actual 2025 spending was well below plan. In fact, in our forecast we had always assumed that the ramp up in infrastructure spending would occur in 2026/27, rather than in 2025/26 as assumed in the government budgets, due to planning delays and the fact that the 2025 budget was only passed in September (see overleaf "Our macro assumptions"). Second, and more importantly, in our report from last December German fiscal stimulus: How effective will it be?, we indeed found evidence that part of the infrastructure fund is used to plug holes in the core budget and that only around half of the funds are planned to be used for spending in growth-intensive infrastructure (which lowers the "fiscal multiplier" of spending - we assume 0.9). Overall, hence, while in our view the ifo study raises valid points, we believe our assumptions for the impact of the fiscal stimulus on growth take those into account. Examining the sensitivity of breakevens to volatility shocks To address this question, as a first pass, we focus on contemporaneous changes of inflation assets to changes in rates volatility, with the view that any repricing should occur without delay. Using short-dated swaption-implied volatility as the explanatory variable, we find that breakevens generally behave like short vol assets in tail moves and exhibit directional asymmetry (responding more to vol increases than vol declines). Moreover, we find that convexity is largely inherited from real-rate dynamics, rather than inflation-specific risk premia. To show how we arrived at that conclusion, we model daily changes in on-the-run breakevens (ΔBE, in bp/day). Rolling beta(Δ30y BE | Δ1m10y), rolling beta(Δ30y RY | Δ1m10y) - 2y rolling window Source: Barclays Research Putting the pieces together To sum up, we find that breakevens are not linearly sensitive to volatility in normal conditions. Their sensitivity emerges nonlinearly; when volatility becomes large enough to force a TIPS sell- off and real rate repricing. In that sense, TIPS themselves are empirically short volatility: real yields may rise sharply in stress scenarios due to hedging flows, balance-sheet constraints, and risk-budget tightening. Breakevens mechanically inherit the opposite exposure, but with more nuance. Losses are small on most days, accelerate in volatility spikes, and are not symmetrically reversed when volatility subsides. The other key takeaway is that breakevens should not be treated as generically fragile to volatility. In orderly policy-path repricing episodes, rising swaption-implied volatility does not reliably compress breakevens and may coincide with stability or widening (especially if the vol shock is inflationary in nature). In essence, hedging breakeven exposure in periods of stress requires protection against real rate volatility, not necessarily inflation-specific factors. As a final point, we see this as a core reason as to why breakevens, and iotas, held in relatively well during the past two significant vol events. Of course, the next episode may be quite different. 2 April 2026 18 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: In limbo

One way to think about it is that breakevens tighten in volatility spikes in part because real yields reprice aggressively, not because inflation-specific risk premia collapse. ...and directional asymmetry Additional evidence comes from examining asymmetry. In full sample regressions of the form ΔBE ~ (Δ1m10y)⁺ + (Δ1m10y)⁻, where (Δ1m10y)⁺ denotes positive vol moves and (Δ1m10y)⁻ denotes negative vol moves, breakevens exhibit cleaner short vol behavior. At the 5y point, the coefficient on positive volatility moves is around −0.18 bp per vol point. In other words, if 1m10y sees a two standard deviation move and the quote rises by ~9.5bp, this modeling would imply that 5y breakevens sell off by ~1.75bp. By contrast, the coefficient on negative volatility moves is small and statistically insignificant; volatility declines do not generate comparably sizeable breakeven moves. The same qualitative pattern holds at the 10y point, with smaller magnitudes, and weakens further at 30y. This asymmetry is characteristic of short-vol exposure, rather than of simple risk-off correlations. records.text: Marija Veitmane 31 March 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Valuations blink, Earnings don’t Geopolitical tensions escalated, oil prices surged, and global equities sold off. The adjustment, however, was driven by higher rates and valuation compression rather than a deterioration in earnings. As a result, investors remained constructive, rotating toward markets and sectors with a more resilient profit outlook. US and Asian markets with higher concentrations of IT stocks stand out as potential winners. As rockets fell across the Middle East—claiming lives and destroying infrastructure—global equities sold off. The move was driven largely by multiple compression, as higher oil prices pushed interest rates up via an inflation shock. Notably, higher oil prices have not yet triggered earnings downgrades, helping explain why investors have stayed relatively constructive. Rather than cutting equity exposure aggressively, they rotated toward areas with more resilient earnings—most notably the US and IT. The shift into US equities has been the largest regional rotation since the conflict began, reflecting an improving earnings outlook. This contrasts with position reductions and earnings downgrades elsewhere, particularly in Europe, where expectations were already weakening before the war. Emerging markets earnings remain relatively robust, supported by Korea, Taiwan, and South Africa, while profitability expectations in China and India continue to deteriorate. Sector

As an example in the US and Germany, policymakers were successful in bringing down rate expectations over a long-term horizon, yields were kept buoyant from investors demanding higher excess returns, i.e., higher term premia to hold long-dated debt. Understanding how interconnected financial markets are is also important. Government expenditures rise through February The financial deficit of the federal budget remained at 1.7% of GDP in February − up 1.1pp since August 2025, driven by higher expenditures. Defence spending in February is 38% higher than a year ago and investment expenditures in the budget are twice their level from a year ago, with most of the increase occurring over the last couple of months (Figures 3-6). Defence-related macro variables: Orders remain close to historical highs In defence, orders in "other transport", which includes military vehicles, remain at historical highs in January (latest data). Orders in weapons and ammunition fell back (to still historically high level), but rose strongly in "explosives" (Figures 7 & 8). Production of "explosives", and in particular weapons and ammunition, increased markedly and hence is starting to affect GDP . Over the next few months, we expect production to pick up further, as companies start to work off the increased orders. For our latest view on Rheinmetall, see this note from Sven Weier. records.text: European Economic Perspectives30 March 2026 ab 3 Tracking stimulus − from budget outlays to production To recap: we track how the stimulus moves through the economy by looking at 59 indicators across different stages of transmission in a heatmap format. First, higher expenditures should become visible in the monthly budget data as the government starts disbursing funds. Second, we expect business confidence in the affected business sectors to pick up in expectation of increased public demand. Third, orders and − with some lag − production data should pick up. Fourth, as capacity utilisation increases, firms may start to expand capacity, which should become visible in employment growth. We track the data for the two sectors that should be most affected: defence-related sectors (including weapons, ammunition, explosives, and other transport equipment, which includes military vehicles) and construction (especially civil engineering). We summarise the respective indicators in a heatmap (Figure 2 F i s c a l s t i m u l u s h e a t m a p ), with green denoting that variables move in the "right" direction, i.e. signalling more spending. The MPC will be acutely aware that this may well leach into prices of traded goods — something it is largely powerless to affect. All the committee can do is hope to anchor business and household inflation expectations by reaffirming its commitment to delivering its medium-term remit. But if it can also seek to anchor market interest rate expectations, and by leaving the probability of outcomes more balanced, it might diminish the upward bias to rate expectations. The challenge for the Bank is likely the scarring from the experience of 2022-23 that saw both the policy rate and inflation spiral higher and the MPC struggle to control rate expectations. Quite rightly, the economics community will point out that the starting point is very different in terms of the underlying policy stance (highly accommodative in 2022 vs restrictive now), the impetus from fiscal policy and the bounce back from COVID to name but three important factors. While we have sympathy for the argument that a rise in unemployment driven by AI could be structural, it is not clear that the Fed would interpret it that way too, especially under the imbalanced reaction function. For instance, NY Fed President Williams suggested that he doesn’t see AI changing the natural rate of unemployment – suggesting a weaker employment picture may be met with a dovish Fed response. Similarly, Fed Governor Waller recently remarked that he was willing to vote for a December cut, based on anecdotes about layoffs (and there are many anecdotes on AI driven layoffs), even while actual jobless claims remained low. AI “macro impact” questions are rising for rates investors. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 30 Mar 2026 08:51:04 ET │ 14 pages US Economics Inflation Weekly – Import prices rising, but with some caveats CITI'S TAKE Our core inflation forecasts are little changed over the last week as we await data following the substantial move higher in global oil prices. Headline inflation will be strong at least over the next two months, with some stickiness in core inflation in March and April likely as well. Some of this strength in core could be due to stronger prices for computer-related goods, which we reviewed a few weeks ago. Computers have also boosted import prices substantially through February data released last week. But we would caution that recent strength in import prices could also reflect post- shutdown measurement issues and changes in tariff rates that may impact selling prices of exporters (i.e. import prices). Inflation expectations and PMI prices increased in March, but not nearly as much as might be expected given the move higher in oil prices. records.text: Second part of report title F O C U S FOCUS 131/03/2026 Silver: Deficits, what deficits? KEY MESSAGES Updating forecasts, but further upside limited: Following the surge to record highs in January, we expect silver prices to remain elevated, trading in range of USD65–75/oz through 2026. However, further upside looks limited given a clear easing in the physical market and signs of institutional investor silver fatigue. We expect the physical market to move into surplus by2027. Silver to underperform: Further out, we expect silver prices to underperform gold, as a weakening industrial demand base dampens sentiment. We expect the gold–silver ratio to return to about 85 before end-2027, while a returning weaker-USD trend should prevent significant downside in H2 2026 and 2027. Slowing industrial demand a key headwind: The adage that ‘high prices are the cure for high prices’ is, we believe, very relevant to silver. In response to the extreme price volatility, we are already seeing aggressive thrifting in industrial end-user sectors, notably solar, EVs and other electronics. We now expect industrial demand to contract by roughly 3% this year and about 6% in 2027. Iran outcome the key immediate risk: Short-term silver prices remain heavily influenced by news flow from conflict in the Middle East. We think rapid progress towards a ceasefire could prompt a brief spike back to USD90/oz, while signs of a potential ground war could spark a drop to USD40–50/ozlevels. BNP PARIBAS GL OBAL

records.text: udget: As JGB yields rise – for example, the 10y yield returning towards its 2026 high of 2.4%, the market is concerned by the rising cost of servicing JGBs for the government. However, this situation is not entirely new. For the 2026 fiscal year, the Ministry of Finance has budgeted JPY13trn in interest, up JPY2.5trn on 2025. Together with the contribution to the redemption (sinking) fund, the share of debt servicing costs in the total budget is already over 25% of total expenditure (see Figure 1). Based on our reverse engineering analysis, the MoF’s budget looks to sufficiently consider the rise in interest rate in 2026, relative to our assumption of a policy rate of 1.25% and a 10y yield averaging 2.5% (see next page). The MoF has been generally conservative in its approach on this, in fact. For example, each year it conducts regular fiscal simulations in January or February for future budgets based on two GDP growth scenarios (high and normal), although the assumptions for JGB servicing costs are similar for both scenarios. Until 2024, it was generally the case that the MoF would initially assume higher interest costs for future years and gradually revise down its cost assumptions. However, from 2025, it stopped doing this (Figure 2). One could argue therefore that scope for MoF conservatism may have diminished. However, the implications for a trading strategy are not straightforward and we set out three factors to discuss such complications. Sources: MoF, BNP Paribas Fig

records.text: ab 30 March 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives Germany: Fiscal stimulus tracker update March Fiscal stimulus tracker updated through March We have recently introduced a fiscal stimulus tracker (see here for details), which gauges to what extent German fiscal stimulus in defence and infrastructure is becoming visible in the macro data over time. To recap, we expect fiscal stimulus to boost German GDP growth by c.60bp in each 2026/27. This growth contribution should be unaffected by the energy shock, which otherwise has increased downside risks to the overall outlook. In this note, we update our heatmap (Figure 2) with data through March and summarise the key developments ( and also briefly discuss a recent study from the ifo institute about the use of the fiscal package, see next para). Overall, the heatmap points to continued progress in transmission of the defence-related stimulus into orders and production. In infrastructure spending, progress remains mainly limited to business confidence. This is also broadly the message from our sector analysts, see below. Despite the slump in overall business confidence in March, according to the ifo index, sentiment in defence and most infrastructure related sectors held up better and the orders outlook has improved. For equity market implications and sector stock screens, see this note from our equity strategy colleagues: German Fiscal Stimulus: Accelerating. The re- allocation may stabilize in April, in our view. We regard that the ‘belly-cheapening’, such as in the 5s10s20s or 7s10s20s, as a structural feature of the curve dynamics as the BoJ’s tightening cycle progresses. While the market has been somewhat divided over the April rate hike because of the likely economic slowdown over the Middle East conflict, a few factors since last week reinforce the BoJ’s tightening stance. First, the central bank now regards supply/demand gap as positive, and second, it raised the lower bound of ‘neutral rate’ by 0.1%, pushing the lowest nominal neutral rate to 1.1% (above 1% or the next level of policy rate after a hike. Third, the BoJ’s Summary of Opinion for March meeting was hawkish, as released on 30 March. We choose to long the 7y leg rather than the 5y. While the 5s7s10s still shows some richness, the current risk-off environment is likely to keep the futures segment priced rich. Page 5 Additionally, the Collateral-in-Lieu (CIL) service, approved in December 2025 by the SEC, has potential to generate more capacity to alleviate borrowing constraints. This service enables the CCP (FICC) to take a lien on the repo collateral instead of requiring a separate margin, thereby reducing overall margin costs. Furthermore, this lien would obviate the need for FICC to require dealers to guarantee the performance of the cash lender they are sponsoring, leading to a reduction in capital costs and freein g up RWA -constrained dealers to intermediate more repo. As more dealers onboard to this new platform over the next year and trading volumes in sponsored GC grow, we anticipate gradual abatement of month - and quarter -end pressures. Should the aforementioned month-end intermediation challenges be resolved fully (SOFR -RRP spreads staying at the average levels between days 7 and 17), we estimate a decline of approximately 1bp in monthly SOFR fixing averages, all else equal. records.text: Shifting probabilities around rate outcomes MPC seeking to shift the balance of risks Pricing for 2026 seems reasonable - but 2027's may be more important for the MPC The probability that GBP 1m rates end 2026 between 3.5-4.0% now sits at around 25%, a 12pp drop since the beginning of March. The probability that it lies between 3.0-3.5% (ie, at least 25bp lower) is now 14%, a 18pp decline over the month. For 2027, the probability shift has been less pronounced, suggesting that we have yet to see a shift in longer-term policy expectations. Figure 3 shows the cumulative probabilities that GBP 1m rates lie below certain levels at the end of 2026 and 2027. This shows more starkly how rate probabilities have decisively shifted for 2026 vs 2027. At the beginning of March, the cumulative probability that GBP 1m rates would be below 4% at the end of 2026 was 84%. This has now dropped to 44%. The relative flattening of the 2026 curve is the consequence of the redistribution of probabilities to higher rates. The median expectation for 2026 has now shifted above 4% and has also increased for 2027, whereas a month ago, both were lower at around 3.5%. Surprisingly not. Why AI is expected to be a significant disinflationary force The case for AI to exert a meaningful drag on inflation is reasonably straightforward. AI is expected to substitute cheap capital / technology for more- expensive labor, driving input costs lower. By leading to sustainably higher productivity growth, it will push unit labor costs substantially lower, weighing on price pressures. To the extent that AI raises the unemployment rate, it will also reduce inflation through increasing labor-market slack, reducing wage growth , and weakening aggregate demand. Finally, AI represents an important equalizing force for entrepreneurs, ushering in countless small businesses with lower barriers to entry that will compete and drive margins lower. This is our understanding of the consensus view on why inflation and rates will be sustainably lower due to AI. But there are countervailing forces to this narrative. In the near term at least, AI has triggered a substantial positive aggregate demand shock, as investment has surged in anything AI -related, including software, chips, computers and peripheral equipment, and data centers. r, if disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz persist, we believe the government is likely to shift its stance and gradually steer policy toward demand restraint. For example, the support measures for petroleum products (gasoline, diesel, heavy fuel oil, kerosene, and aviation fuel) that have been in place since March 19 are explicitly positioned as emergency mitigation measures to smooth sudden price shocks. While it is unlikely that the government would abruptly terminate fuel subsidies, there is a high likelihood that the framework will be reviewed so as to allow fuel prices, including gasoline, to rise gradually in line with market prices. Under the current system, 100% of the portion of gasoline retail prices above ¥170 per liter is subsidized without an upper limit. Maintaining this structure over an extended period poses significant challenges from the perspective of restraining energy consumption. From a fiscal standpoint as well, the current fuel-support framework is difficult to characterize as sustainable. Based on the FY2026 petroleum product demand outlook published in April 2025 by METI’s Petroleum Product Demand Outlook Study Group, simple estimates suggest that if the current subsidy levels were maintained for a full year, the fiscal cost would reach approximately ¥5 trillion (Exhibit 8 ). Should crude oil prices continue to rise, the fiscal burden could expand further.

Relatively high levels of crude oil reserves Japan maintains a relatively high level of oil reserves, making it less vulnerable to immediate supply constraints in the event of short-term disruptions. Even during periods of international market turmoil, Japan can secure a buffer period to adjust supply-demand balances and implement policy responses. Japan’s oil reserves are managed through a three-tiered structure: national reserves, private-sector reserves, and joint reserves with oil-producing countries. As of the end of January 2026, the total reserve stood at approximately eight months’ worth (about seven months by IEA standards), according to the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy. The breakdown is as follows: national reserves cover 146 days (approximately 270 million barrels of crude oil and products), private-sector reserves cover 96 days (about 170 million barrels), and joint reserves with oil-producing countries cover six days (about 12 million barrels), totaling approximately 460 million barrels. Some overseas reports have suggested that Japan’s oil reserves amount to only about three months’ worth, which has sparked discussion among investors. Figure 1 plots rolling two-year betas of breakevens on Δ1m10y swaption-implied vol, across tenors, under baseline and controlled specifications. Several features are immediately apparent. Predictably, the exposure is front-end dominated: 5y breakevens show the largest swings in vol beta, 10y exhibits more muted moves, and 30y the smallest response. More notably, the exposure is not stable and does not even show a consistent sign. Betas fluctuate around zero and move between positive and negative regimes over time; ie, breakevens are not persistently short vol in a linear sense. Figures 2-4 show that controlling for contemporaneous real rate changes materially alters the estimated volatility exposure, often shifting the coefficient substantially and, in some regimes, reversing its sign. This sensitivity underscores that breakevens do not embed a stable linear short vol exposure; rather, apparent volatility sensitivity largely reflects real rate dynamics, which have varying correlation with volatility across regimes. The government has also started releasing national oil reserves at prices that predate the escalation of the Middle-East situation . Thanks to the combination of subsidies and reserve releases, the retail price of gasoline will be suppressed below last year's average level. Higher energy prices due to the conflict imply significant rises in electricity and gas bills for the summer season, when electricity usage increases due to cooling demand. However, we think the government is likely to reduce households’ bills for the summer season by reviving the electricity and gas subsidies that ended in March. Significant fiscal cost: The Japanese economy can avoid immediate and dramatic impacts in terms of either energy supply and prices, but prolonged subsidies to suppress energy prices would result in substantial fiscal costs. The gasoline subsidy, which was restarted at JPY30.2 per liter, has already been increased to JPY49.8, and if this level of provision continues, it will require about JPY500bn per month. The electricity and gas bill subsidies required a budget of over JPY500bn for the January–March period, and since current oil and LNG prices far exceed the levels at the time of price determination for that quarter, the budget for keeping a similar level of electricity and gas bills will be substantially larger. records.text: . Based on historical GPT diffusion patterns (David, 1990; Brynjolfsson et al., 2021), 5–7 years is typically when measurable productivity gains begin appearing in macro data. Baily, Brynjolfsson, & Korinek (2023) project AI could add 0.4–0.9pp to annual labor productivity growth, which would translate to meaningful downward pressure on unit labor costs and thus prices. • Services inflation moderation: Services constitute roughly 60% of the CPI basket and have been the primary driver of post-pandemic inflation persistence. AI is disproportionately suited to automating or augmenting service-sector tasks (Eloundou et al., 2023), suggesting it could address the stickiest component of inflation. Healthcare administration, financial services, legal services, education, and government services are all areas where AI could reduce costs. • Supply chain and logistics optimization: AI-driven improvements in demand forecasting, inventory management, routing, and supply chain coordination could reduce goods-sector costs, compounding the services-side effects. • Scenario D tail risk (20%): The probability of meaningful deflation (−0.5pp or more) is substantial at the 5-year horizon. This reflects the possibility of faster-than-expected AI capability improvements (e.g., toward more autonomous AI agents) and rapid adoption. Import prices will not directly reflect tariffs but would capture any effects of exporters lowering their selling prices to help offset tariff costs for importers. Exporters did lower prices (import prices fell) at various points for goods like apparel. A rise in import prices in February could reflect that exporters are no longer keeping their selling prices abnormally low, as IEEPA tariffs were replaced with generally lower 10% Section 122 tariffs. For instance, import prices from China have risen in the last two months after falling substantially over the last year. Mechanically, average import prices in March may also be strong again for this reason (if prices changed later in February after the Supreme Court ruling). But aside from these considerations, a key detail of January/February import prices is strength in computers and electronics, which have largely not been impacted by tariffs. records.text: market structure continues to favor the non-centrally cleared bilateral repo (NCCBR) segment despite the benefits that central clearing offers, such as mitigated counterparty risks and balance sheet netting for dealers. This preference stems from the additional legal and operational costs associated with central clearing, alongside the required margins calculated via strict Value -at- Risk (VaR) models imposed by the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation (FICC). In contrast, non -cleared repo, particularly in the NCCBR segment, offers greater flexibility in terms, with the majority of transactions featuring no haircut and more discretionary margins. The NCCBR segment is relatively opaque and not captured by SOFR’s calculation, though it currently makes up a significant proportion of dealers’ lending to hedge funds, most of which occurs at higher rates than the current SOFR distribution. The central clearing mandate is poised to integrate more activity in this segment into the SOFR calculation, which will have the technical impact of biasing SOFR higher toward dealer-hedge fund client trades. The two key effects will be a wider SOFR-fed funds spread (SERFF more negative), and a compression of the GC - SOFR spread. When the Middle East conflict began, investors quickly started pricing in interest rate hikes for most G10 central banks. Inflation fears took centre stage, overshadowing concerns about economic growth. Now, after five weeks, expectations are rising that reopening the Strait of Hormuz will require additional time. The shock to physical oil supply from the Iran War surpasses any previous post-war oil shocks, including those from the 1970s. If the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, it will increasingly impact global economic growth, with some countries being especially vulnerable. Notably, those most exposed have the highest likelihood of rate hikes priced in one year ahead. Whether Iran and the US reach a deal or the war persists, we believe the best approach is to push back on current rate market expectations for the G10 central banks. Portfolio. records.text: SSA: most vulnerable region to food risks Loic Porte MLI (UK) Tatonga Rusike MLI (UK) SSA countries are big importers of food products and the weight of these products in the inflation basket is much larger on average than in other emerging markets. Increases in fertilizer prices raise the costs of food both produced domestically and imported from abroad. On average (in our coverage) 42% of the population cannot afford sufficient calories, meaning that any increase in food prices can have extreme health and social consequences. South Africa: food prices steady for now South Africa’s fertilizer market is facing near‑term price pressure due to global supply fears stemming from the Iran–Israel–US conflict. South Africa relies on imports for about 80% of its fertilizer needs and having imported US$1.14 billion in 2025. Fuel and fertilizers together make up about 50% of grain production input costs, and while fertilizer prices have risen 15–20%, fuel costs are set to jump nearly 30% on 1 April. Because fertilizer demand peaks only when the planting season resumes in October 2026, current increases are driven more by concerns rather than actual shortages. At a high level, the indicators reveal whether real -money investors are leaning into or leaning out of a given FX factor (e.g. carry, value, momentum). The indicators aggregate single currency indicators, including the Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) and Foreign Exchange Holdings Indicator (FXHI), into broader factor aggregates. This translates into just ~3% of the daily run-rate volume seen pre-war. Who is crossing the strait? The four vessels include two Indian LPG tankers and one crude oil tanker journeying to Pakistan. While Iran has made select exceptions for vessels from friendly countries to cross the Strait, the risks remain quite elevated. On March 27th , three Chinese containerships (COSCO) attempted to cross the Strait but then reversed course. Two of the ships are again attempting to cross the Strait today. Meanwhile, The UK Maritime Trade Operations Center has stated that 11 vessels did cross the Strait last Saturday. While it is unclear how many of these are tankers, it is possible that a few tankers have transited the Strait with their AIS switched off. Iranian shipments Oil shipments via the SoH consist almost entirely of Iran's exports, primarily done via its dark fleet (i.e., tankers with their AIS switched off). Iran's exports this month are estimated to be close to its pre-war levels of ~1.6 mb/d. Iran's revenues are surging as Brent prices have surged above $100 per barrel and the discount of its oil exports to the benchmark has narrowed to its lowest level in the last 10 months. records.text: ECB, BoJ, Morgan Stanley Research forecasts The differences between those scenarios bear attention. Higher oil prices mean higher inflation in the near term, so all else equal, there should be higher policy rates. But all else is never equal. The path to an extended hiking cycle requires not only higher inflation but also enough growth that makes second-round inflationary risks credible. That path could come from a fiscal response that tries to shield households and businesses from the rising costs. Timing becomes critical here. Our research has been consistent in noting that inflation upside precedes growth downside. The Fed likely has a bias to “look through” transitory inflation, but it will take time to be convinced of that path. The ECB and others are poised to hike on inflation alone, and any shift in policy to address growth must come later, implying further potential shifts to front end pricing. The fact that many economies, particularly in Asia, already use fiscal mechanisms to smooth energy prices domestically, is embedded in our policy rate forecasts. Overall, however, our assessment continues to be that central bankers and investors alike are focussing too much on inflation risks and not enough on growth risks.

records.text: If the US were to pull out of the current Middle East conflict but with average US retail gasoline prices rising above $4/gallon1, one can envisage a scenario where the US introduces an export cap or ban on both crude oil and petroleum products to lower US domestic prices and prevent leakage of either crude oil or petroleum products outside of the US through exports. The administration ruled out a ban in mid-March (Politico, March 19). Downsides to such restrictions are widely discussed (e.g., Columbia University, March 18). However, if oil, gasoline and diesel prices stay high, an eventual cap or ban on US exports can’t be completely ruled out. While one scenario could be to just restrict gasoline and diesel exports that matter the most to consumers, it could leave the potential leakage problem unaddressed. If restrictions are only imposed on petroleum products, then US crude oil producers would have incentives to export more crude oil, while domestic refiners with US crude oil offtake might also want to export more of the crude and refine less due to greater scope for profit in the former, unless the government restricts exports. But such a restriction would effectively amount to restricting crude oil exports. In addition, if there are no restrictions on crude oil exports, then crude oil prices would be higher but petroleum product prices in the US would not be as high as elsewhere globally. A reduction in refining margins could lead to lower refinery run rates in the US.

In response, the country implemented a series of policy measures, including the establishment of a national petroleum reserve system and fundamental improvements in energy efficiency. As a result, Japan has moved away from a structure in which supply disruptions immediately lead to physical shortages or economic shutdowns. Today, it has built a system that combines inventory, domestic refining capacity, and fuel price stabilization measures to absorb short-term external shocks within the scope of price adjustments. The following points, in particular, explain why Japan’s economy has relative strengths in the face of short-term oil shocks: 1. High domestic refining capacity for gasoline and diesel Japan maintains a consumption-site refining model based on crude oil imports and domestic refining. The vast majority of gasoline demand is met by domestic refineries, and under normal conditions Japan’s dependence on imports of gasoline is extremely low. Japan is also a net exporter of diesel fuel in normal times, exporting mainly to Australia and other Asian economies. While diesel, like gasoline, is primarily domestically refined, domestic demand is smaller than for gasoline. In 2025, diesel imports totaled ¥102.7 billion, while exports reached ¥482.2 billion, resulting in a net export surplus of roughly ¥380 billion. 2. Relatively high levels of crude oil reserves Japan maintains

Rates Fixed Income Blog Date 30 March 2026 The term premium is at a decade high. But is it too high? No. Some commentators have argued that the UST10Y is cheap because measures of term premia are high relative to recent history. It is factually correct that term premia are close to a decade high. The DB term premium (5s10s slope + 20% short in 2s) has indeed risen from below 50bp in 2022, when we argued that term premia were likely to be on a secular uptrend, to above 100bp today. But that does not mean that the term premium is too high. Indeed, in an environment with persistent negative supply shocks and structurally easier fiscal policy, term premia should increase. During negative supply shocks, bonds are not good hedges for equities as higher inflation is bad for both bonds and equities. As the hedging properties are eroded, bonds should have a higher risk premium. Separately, significant upward pressure on deficits will reduce excess savings and thereby put upward pressure on term premia and equilibrium rates. Source: Citi Research, OPEC, OilX Source: Citi Research, OPEC, OilX There are buffers to cover current shortages, though they are more short-term. First, a drawdown of stranded, restricted Russian and Iran oil would help to partly mitigate the supply tightness, but they were largely taken in March. Second, SPR drawdowns coordinated by the IEA have helped, though Asian countries, most exposed to Middle Eastern oil and product export cuts, are not direct recipients of such drawdowns. Indeed, Jan-Feb 2026 export volume was at its highest Jan-Feb volume on record, and unsurprisingly, given silver price trends YTD, January made up the bulk of that. These trends challenge concerns that the new licensing regime would constrain Chinese silver exports. In fact, more companies are now licensed to export silver over the next two years compared to the previous licensing period. China’s time as a net importer likely limited: China has been a net exporter of silver for 52 of the 62 months since January 2021. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. Source: ECB, Haver Analytics, Barclays Research This likely represents a reversal of the dynamic witnessed during the ECB's asset purchase period when TARGET2 balances between core and periphery countries widened, ie, Germany's TARGET2 claims increased while Italy's TARGET2 liabilities increased. With the ECB pursuing QT and hence reducing its footprint on the EGB market, foreign investors have stepped in to fill the void. For example, over the past two years, the share of BTPs held by investors outside Italy has increased by c.7%, completely offsetting the decline in the ownership share of the Eurosystem. We see a similar dynamic in Spain ( Who bought EGBs in Q4-25?). These cross-border flows through the Eurosystem's payments architecture have proved to be a net injection of liquidity into more reserve-strained banking systems. This analysis, hence, underscores that at a country level, other factors beyond just the reduction in TL TROs and monetary policy portfolios have been influencing the evolution of excess liquidity

Redemption costs: The MoF also budgets for JGB redemption costs in its annual budget based on the ‘60- year redemption rule’. Under this rule, the MoF contributes one sixtieth of the outstanding amount to the Redemption (sinking) Fund special account. This special account also manages the cash flow related to JGBs, including the actual redemption, which of course differs from this contribution to redemption. JPY jawboning and rate divergence Japan’s Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs recently warned speculators that authorities may intervene if current FX conditions persist. Japan imports 90% of its energy so its economy is much more sensitive to an energy shock. This is enough to compel a hawkish shift among officials. records.text: United States: Inflation Markets Are breakevens still short vol? In light of recent episodes of market stress (eg, Liberation Day, Iran conflict), we examine the sensitivity of inflation assets, particularly BEs, to rates volatility. For BEs, we find a non-linear and asymmetric sensitivity to rates vol in recent years. Is inflation short vol? As a general truism about inflation markets, it is broadly assumed that "breakevens are short vol" in the sense that when volatility (either realized or implied) jumps, we should expect to see breakevens underperform. Intuitively, we see two channels through which this may occur: 1) higher vol = tighter financial conditions, presaging weaker forward inflation pressure, and/or 2) higher vol = balance sheet de-risking, which would press iotas wider (and lead breakevens to underperform CPI swaps). Indeed, the negative relationship makes sense, and we include the VIX as an explanatory variable in the 10y breakeven fair-value model in our Inflation-Linked Daily — unsurprisingly, it has a statistically significant negative coefficient. However, recent episodes of heightened volatility — namely April 2025 and March 2026 — have not necessarily seen the same underperformance of breakevens as one might have feared, especially via the second channel noted above. This begs the wonky but important question: are breakevens and/or CPI swap positions still implicitly short vol? In this note, we dive into the deep end on the topic. Examining the sensitiv

Within this, India dominates, accounting for roughly 40% of jewellery and around 67% of silverware demand, driven by seasonal trends in weddings and gifting. This demand has a positive correlation with rising precious metals prices, whereby elevated gold prices prompt substitute demand for silver. With silver prices easing following January’s rally, we forecast jewellery demand for silver to rise modestly in 2026, by 1–2% to 198.7 moz, while demand from silverware remains flat at 45.3 moz. If production cuts in ethylene and propylene intensify, the impact is likely to spread beyond resins such as polyethylene, polypropylene, and polystyrene to downstream sectors where substitution is difficult. These include industrial solvents, synthetic rubber, synthetic fibers, paints, adhesives, detergent feedstocks, packaging materials, and materials used in medical and hygiene products. Exhibit 7 uses the medium-level classification (108 sectors) of the input–output tables to identify the top 20 sectors with the highest dependence on chemical-related industries, including indirect linkages, based on input structures and the extent to which chemical production is required through supply chains. Even industries that appear non-chemical at first glance—such as passenger vehicles and beverages—exhibit a high degree of embedded dependence on chemical industries due to the cumulative effects of indirect inputs via components, materials, containers, packaging, and raw materials. That said, this indicator reflects static relationships based on normal-times input structures and does not directly capture actual production adjustments or the magnitude of impacts under supply- constrained conditions.

However, in a blog post published earlier this week — on which Perli is listed as an author — the Fed appears to have subtly but meaningfully revised that guidance. 5 While much of the content closely mirrors Perli’s earlier remarks, the language around timing was tweaked: a reduction would no longer occur “after April, ” but instead would begin “with the purchase period spanning mid-April to mid-May. ” Why the change? We can only speculate. One possibility is that the Fed reconsidered after quarter‑end pressures failed to materialize and there was effectively no demand for cash via the SRP . After all, the Fed spent much of last year encouraging SRP usage when it was economical to do so. It just so happens that it is no longer economical — even at quarter‑end. That, in turn, suggests the Fed is not running its balance sheet as efficiently as it would like. Alternatively, perhaps the initial remarks were intended in a general sense rather than as precise guidance given the technical details of the mid-month to mid-month purchase period can be confusing to communicate, in which case the blog post intention may have been to more clearly articulate when this change would happen. records.text: Oil Monitor 02 April 2026 Citi Research 4 Iran has imposed a so-called ‘transit fee’ on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz (CNBC, April 1), but its implementation is still subject to many questions. Although buyers of crude oil and petroleum products might agree to pay the fee, due to the nature of FOB (Free on Board) contracts, some Gulf oil exporters might not want to be subject to the influence of such tolls, particularly for geopolitical reasons (CNBC TV via YouTube, March 25) Assuming only some Middle Eastern exporting countries are agreeable with their oil buyers paying the transit fee but other peer exporting countries are not, then the resulting transit disruptions could lead world supply to be short 8-mb/d. In such a scenario, the amount of crude oil exported could fall from 13.9-mb/d in our base scenario outlined above to 11.7-mb/d and the amount of petroleum product exported could fall from 1.9 to 0.7-mb/d, for a total crude and petroleum product exports of 12.4-mb/d. Existing US restrictions on Iranian oil exports could complicate any such toll arrangements by Iran. President Trump floated the idea of the US getting involved jointly with Iran in controlling the Hormuz strait (CNBC, March 27). Could existing restrictions on Iranian oil be removed in such a scenario? Based on our reverse engineering, MoF’s budget looks to cover the cost sufficiently in 2026, relative to our forecast of policy rate to 1.25% and 10y yield averaging at 2.5% (detail on the next page). In fact, MoF has been generally conservative. For example, it does regular fiscal simulation in January or February every year for the future budget based on a couple of GDP growth (high and normal) scenarios, although the assumption for JGB service cost is largely the same for both scenarios. Until 2024, it was generally the case that the MoF initially assumes higher interest costs for the future years and gradually revises down. However, from 2025, the MoF no longer revised down the cost. For 2026 and later, the cost has been adjusted upwards (Figure 2). Therefore, we may say that the room for MoF’s conservatism may have become smaller going forward. records.text: 3 Insights Information Classification: General About PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. records.text: Europe: Money Markets Reserves reflections Eurosystem reserve drain is into its fourth year running and the process has been uneventful so far. We show how cross- border flows have supported excess liquidity levels in reserve scarce countries. A slowdown or reversal in these flows could raise concerns over fragmented reserve distribution. The glacial decline in G3 central bank reserves, underway since 2022, hit an inflection point with the Fed’s decision to launch reserve management purchases late last year. This once again signalled the Fed's limited tolerance for funding market pressures, also given reserves as percentage of banking assets were close to their 'critical' threshold ( Figure 1). Our US colleagues expect these reserve management purchases (RMPs) to reach a steady state run-rate of $20bn/m. Beyond this near-term development, the nomination of Kevin Warsh to the Fed has sharpened the focus on the Fed’s balance sheet and how (if at all) can it be shrunk again. It is therefore quite likely that USD plumbing dynamics would remain a focus area for the market in the months ahead and would be central in determining if reserve divergence would persist and to what scale. Relative to the Fed’s pre-emptive risk-management-driven ample-reserves framework, the two central banks on this side of the pond have clearly chosen to tread a different path. records.text: pipeline inflationary pressures may soon make their presence felt. Given the constant whipsaw on headlines, the market environment remains unfriendly towards any directional (long or short) positions in EUR rates. Thus, we continue to hold our EUR2s5s10s fly position. But what could a de-escalation look like in the EUR rates space? In terms of the shape of the swaption-implied probability distribution for ECB policy rates as of end-2026, there have been two distinct changes over the past month: it has shifted right (ie, the modal outcome has shifted towards the ECB's leaving its good place this year) and the right tail has fattened. In our view, a credible de-escalation in the Gulf conflict should narrow the right tail even if it does not shift the distribution leftwards all the way back to February levels. The market is likely to continue to work with a base case of 1-2 rate hikes from the ECB this year, with some tail of a larger adjustment. It is precisely the repricing of this tail narrower that would help rates volatility decline and could support steepeners and EGB compression trades even if the steady state on policy rates is higher than 2%. In conclusion, for every pocket of EUR rates, the 'shock' factor remains the pricing of the ECB's policy path and its distribution, which in itself is a function of spot geopolitical developments and their influence on pipeline inflationary pressures. Another factor we highlighted in a recent note is that the supply of incremental short futures positions to meet the demand for long overlays by asset managers has increasingly come from dealers rather than leveraged funds over the past year — likely a consequence of bank deregulation (see here), and that implies there would be potentially less pullback during quarter-end dates as leveraged funds require relatively less financing for their long-cash positions. So what does the benign quarter-end tell us about reserve demand? First, reserves appeared to move into a steeper part of the demand curve when reserves were only about $80bn below current levels ($2.960tn versus $3.036tn). That suggests repo pressures may not be far off, particularly once the TGA moves sharply higher in late April and after the tax deadline. Second, at the same time, markets are behaving as if reserves are now above ample — arguably in abundant territory — with repo pressures all but nonexistent at quarter-end. These observations appear at odds with one another. Taken together, however, they suggest that the “ample” zone is a very narrow window of reserves, and that the transition from abundance to scarcity is likely quite rapid. 2 April 2026 19 FICC Research Interest Rates 2 April 2026 Samuel Earl + 1 212 526 5426 samuel.earl@barclays.com BCI, US

Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. A 10% persistent increase in the oil prices does push up core inflation by 4-5bp over the coming year, but it also pushes up the unemployment rate by a similar magnitude over the following couple of years ( Figure 4). A 50% increase in oil prices could therefore push up core inflation by 20-25bp, but also lift the unemployment rate by about 20bp. Over time, core inflation is modeled to come back down to pre-war baseline, but there is an overhang of a weaker labor market. Balance sheet benefits and dealer intermediation While the technical implementation of central clearing is likely to bias SOFR fixings higher, there are important offsetting factors to consider. One of these considerations is the impact on dealer intermediation capacity, with the OFR estimating that central clearing would have netted over $200bn in repo positions in August last year. During periods of heightened demand for balance sheet netting, such as month - and quarter -ends, dealers push clients into centrally cleared repo activity. However, this introduces RWA capital constraints for some banks, as the dominant sponsored central clearing service (in which dealers sponsor clients into FICC) requires dealers to guarantee the performance of the sponsored member. Risk of Supply-Chain Disruptions Triggered by Tightness in Basic Chemical Products Disruptions are emerging in the procurement of naphtha, which has a high dependence on the Middle East, prompting domestic manufacturers to already lower operating rates at ethylene facilities and implement production cuts. Our chemicals analyst Takato Watabe notes that “if tensions in the Middle East persist, ethylene production could decline significantly from May onward” (Petrochemical Majors: JPCA Stats (Feb): Ethylene Production Could Drop Sharply from May Depending on Middle East Situation (24 Mar 2026)). Once the initial phase in which inventories function as a buffer has passed, supply constraints could materialize rapidly. A scenario in which price increases and volume constraints occur simultaneously—leading to a decline in utilization rates across the entire supply chain—represents a key downside risk. At a press conference on March 24, Yukishiro Kudo, Chairman of the Japan Petrochemical Industry Association, stated that current inventories amount to roughly four months of domestic demand for polyethylene and around three months for polypropylene, and that ethylene production facilities can be “just barely maintained” through April (NHK). Conversely, this suggests that the risk of binding supply constraints will rise as time passes. We expect central banks to deliver fewer rate hikes than markets currently imply, as we generally expect limited second round effects to core inflation and growth concerns increasingly come to the fore. We look for the Fed to keep rates unchanged this year––a call we have held since before the conflict. Recent market moves have closed some of the gap with our forecast due to the Fed’s recognition of sticker inflation. At the same time, the FOMC has made it clear that it will take time to understand the implications of a shock that has two-sided risks. For EMs, which are often compelled to hike in response to financial stability concerns, a steady Fed should help cap the pressure. Moreover, the starting point for inflation is favor- able and many EMs were still biased to ease before the con- flict. As a result, the policy response so far has been one of increased caution rather than outright hawkishness. We’ve added one hike in the Philippines and mostly delayed rate cuts elsewhere. Markets have repriced EM central banks in a more hawkish direction by raising the pricing of year-end pol- icy rates by 90bp on average, led by high-yielders (Türkiye, Hungary, and Brazil). These would likely exacerbate the drag on consumers and boost the risk for a recession. records.text: 2 EEMEA Viewpoint | 30 March 2026 Beyond energy, watch ags: 40%+ upside Daryna Kovalska MLI (UK) We see material upside risks for agriculture prices: under the case of the Iran conflict extending into 3Q 2026, wheat prices could be c.35% higher in 2026, and corn c.45%. If geopolitical tensions extend through H2 2026, prices could be another 15-20% higher on top of that. Beyond production risks from a fertilizer crisis and higher energy/freight costs, crises trigger grain stockpiling and elevate wheat as the key hedge (Exhibit 2). Iran conflict has more severe global implications for fertilizer than in 2022 Hormuz is a critical chokepoint for global fertilizer supply. Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE collectively account for 50% of global sulfur exports and 34% of urea, with most shipments transiting the Strait of Hormuz (Exhibit 3). In addition, China and India, among the world’s biggest producers of urea, also heavily rely on Middle East LNG, with gas typically accounting for 60-80% of production costs. Together, China, India and the Middle East make up around 65-70% of global urea supply. The strong linkage between gas and nitrogen fertilizers suggests further upside risks for fertilizer prices should gas prices rise further. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW Dav id Wilson, Senior Commodities Strategist | BNP Paribas Singapore Branch 31/03/2026 Speculative futures positioning loses influence: CME net speculative futures length has been on a downtrend since June 2025. To put this into perspective, net speculative length has averaged the equivalent of about 46 moz YTD versus a weekly average last year of about 164 moz. This can be partly explained by the CME raising margin requirements from 15% to 18% in early 2026, increasing the cost of holding leveraged long positions, but the more significant cause has been the sharp increase in silver price volatility since early Q4 2025. Funds switch focus: There was notable upside call buying through H2 2025– January 2026 as funds used options to express bullish silver views. This stalled as the Iran conflict began, with skew suggesting a focus on downside protection. Physical investment demand mixed: Silver bar and coin demand was strong through Q4 2025 and early January, and we expect this to continue. However, physical ETF silver holdings have been on a downtrend since 23 December 2025, with 68 moz of outflows since then – partly due to profit-taking. We think extreme volatility in silver prices since early December has disincentivised physical silver exposure, with gold favoured as a longer -term portfolio diversification asset. With their call of ‘get ready to repo’ , the BoE and, to a large extent, the ECB have signalled that their primary plan is to supply reserves to the system through borrowing operations even though the ECB aims to launch a structural bond portfolio at some point. While both institutions have put guardrails in place (and there is more to come from ECB) in order to ensure orderly money market functioning as the search for the point of reserve scarcity continues, neither central bank is yet to be truly tested. Specifically, the ECB’s reserve drain process has indeed been like ‘ watching paint dry’ , despite concerns around the fragmented nature of excess reserve distribution between and within countries. Now, in its fourth year running, aggregate Eurosystem excess liquidity has fallen below €2.4trn, a 49% decline from the peak. While much of the initial decline (from Q4 22) was driven by repayments of TL TRO-III loans and hence resulted in step declines in excess liquidity, the reserve drain has progressively become much smoother, driven primarily by the QT process which would remain the main source of reserve drain going forward ( Figure 3) (See latest blog post from ECB on how banks are adjusting to declining reserves). 2 April 2026 33 FICC Research Interest Rates 2 April 2026 Rohan Khanna +44 (0) 20 7773 0533 rohan.khanna1@barclays.com Barclays, UK

Energy supply not a problem for now: Japan’s oil stockpiles (national, private, and joint ones with producer countries) were equivalent to 235 days of demand as at 29 March. Therefore, there is little concern about a near- term supply shortage of oil itself. The government has also lifted the operating restrictions on coal-fired power plants that had been introduced to reduce carbon emissions. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

records.text: Derivatives Strategy Not fully out of the woods Top-left implied vols remain elevated relative to near‑term rate outcomes, with pricing still embedding meaningful two‑way tail risk. We recommend a 3m1y broken receiver fly. US swap spreads have found support amid orderly front‑end funding conditions, though the near-term upside is capped. US options Vol markets have begun to stabilize, with implied vol off the highs of early March across the surface. The decreases are most noticeable on the LHS of the surface, with 1y1y vol falling from nearly 115bp/y to about 100bp/y (Figure 1). This is mostly the result of the cleanup of positions, in our view, given that the rise in volatility was sparked mainly by stop-outs of option structures that were positioned for Fed hikes (payer ladders and ratio spreads). But vol is still quite elevated overall, particularly on the LHS, and is likely to decrease further even without a large decline in oil prices, especially as the market gets more clarity on the Fed's reaction function. In particular, some parts of the vol surface such as 3m1y (at around 95bp/y) seem especially elevated relative to the range of plausible outcomes over the next three months, when the Fed is most likely simply to remain on hold. Forward rates are now priced for less than one cut over the next year, with vol being high mainly because the market is pricing in both tails to be significant. Aggregating details across states, we note that prices for “electricity, gas, and other fuels” seem to have risen a bit less than we thought, potentially only around 2.5%M vs our forecast at 4.1%M. Food inflation was instead a bit higher than we expected at 0.9%Y after 1.1%Y in February (vs MSe 0.7%M), which offsets for headline the smaller-than-expected surge in energy inflation. Core CPI inflation was in line with our forecast at 2.5%Y, stable from February. Services inflation was also stable at 3.2%Y, while we expected a slight increase to 3.3%Y on an uptick in inflation for tourism-related items (air fares, package holidays, accommodation, “PAA”) and only a small decline in underlying services inflation. Specifically, we estimate that services-excluding-PAA declined to 3.0%Y from 3.15%Y, while we had expected a decline to around 3.1%Y. records.text: MEs), financing conditions could deteriorate further, raising the risk of an increase in bankruptcies and business closures. Against the backdrop of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, fuel and transportation costs are expected to rise, alongside higher prices for petrochemical products and construction materials. As a result, the rate of increase in the wholesale price index could accelerate sharply in the period ahead. Meanwhile, in a phase of slowing demand, SMEs with limited pricing power are likely to face persistent difficulty in fully passing on rising costs. On March 27, in light of escalating tensions in the Middle East, the government issued an emergency request to financial institutions to ensure thorough support for SMEs facing financing strains. In the statement titled “Financial Responses in Light of the Middle East Situation,” jointly issued by Prime Minister Takaichi and Minister of State for Fiscal and Financial Affairs Satsuki Katayama, financial institutions were urged to proactively monitor business conditions—including through the establishment and operation of consultation desks—for SMEs, small and micro enterprises, SME cooperatives, as well as mid-sized and large firms, and to provide careful and empathetic responses to financing consultations so as to prevent serious disruptions to business funding. This suggests that downside economic risks are entering a phase that warrants policy intervention.

records.text: M Idea 2 Japan Under an Oil Shock: Short-Term Resilience and the Risk of Nonlinear Deterioration We believe that downside risks to the growth outlook are increasing due to the turmoil in the Middle East (Japan Economics: GDP Forecast Table Update (After Revised Oct-Dec 2025 GDP): Uncertainty Remains High (10 Mar 2026)). Depending on future developments, we may revise our GDP forecast at an appropriate time. However, at this stage, we think it is more important to present the framework through which we assess the impact than to change the numerical forecast itself. Below, we outline our basic thinking. Japan’s economy has a relative time buffer compared to other Asian countries Despite facing the same shock from the Middle East situation, Japan remains one of the few countries in Asia that has not yet experienced major economic disruption. In countries such as the Philippines, Thailand, and Australia, physical shortages of gasoline and diesel have already emerged. Some emerging Asian economies are entering a phase where they are restricting fuel quantities and refueling frequency, increasing holidays for government agencies, limiting driving days, and prioritizing fuel distribution to key industries— measures that constrain mobility, labor, and industrial activity itself. In contrast, while there is a sense of tightness in the supply of certain fuels such as heavy oil in Japan, the supply of fuels for consumers—particularly gasoline and diesel—has been maintained. records.text: ab 2 April 2026 Global Research Global Rates Strategy Spillovers in 2y rates across G-10: the UK's special relationship US spillovers return as short-term rate expectations shift higher Data dependency of central banks and the potential for another global tightening cycle in response to the energy shock could bring back spillovers from the US. Front-end yields have risen by around 60 bps in response to the conflict in the Middle East, mostly from expectations of higher short-term rates over the next two years (Figure 1C h a n g e i n 2 - y e a r y i e l d s a c r o s s G 1 0 r a t e s i n M a r c h ). Curves have bear flattened after the surge in energy prices, echoing historic responses to an inflation shock. How a potential growth slowdown will be priced remains to be seen. Historically it has taken time for yields to price growth slowdowns. A further surge in energy prices could prompt rate markets to shift the focus from inflation worries to growth concerns. Gilts have been the most vulnerable to the repricing of front-end rates, followed by Italy. We have also seen higher term premium priced in the US, UK, Italy and Spain. We attribute roughly a quarter to a third of the pricing of the term premium in Gilts, Bonos and BTPs to the uncertainty around the Fed's reaction function to the inflation shock (Figure 2S p i l l o v e r s f r o m U S 2 - y e a r t e r m p r e m i u m t o t h e r e s t o f G 1 0 ). The 50th percentile is constrained to equal a neutral position relative to benchmark, such that percentiles above the 50 th represent overweights, values below represent underweights. Due to the nature of the specific fixed income data series, we percentile our Sovereign Bond Flows in normal fashion, with no constraint on what constitutes a 50th percentile reading, again over a five-year history to attain a sense of scale. For the IMM percentiles we do one additional transformation to the raw data on flows and positions. To account for the rapid growth in trading volumes we scale both flows and positions by the total open interest before calculating the percentiles. Proprietary Indicator Definitions Our proprietary measures of investor behaviour model the flows represented in the aggregated portfolios of sophisticated investors, which account for approximately 15% of the world’s investable securities. The Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) is a measure of the currency flows of institutional investors. It is designed to gauge institutional investor sentiment toward a set of developed and emerging markets currencies. The indicator is derived primarily from longer-dated forward contract flows as these have been shown to be significantly correlated with currency returns.
